    • Gold and silver

    Real rates and the dollar

    Gold pays no interest or dividend. So the cost of holding it depends on the return available elsewhere, especially the real rate of interest after inflation. Gold often tends to move against real rates and the dollar, but that relationship has clearly weakened in some periods.

    What is a real rate?

    A real rate is roughly the nominal rate minus expected inflation: real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation expectations. For example, if a bond yields 4% and inflation is expected to be 2.5%, the real return is about 1.5% (illustrative numbers).

    The measure most watched in markets is the yield on US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS). The 10-year TIPS yield is used as the market's version of the 10-year real rate. The difference between the ordinary 10-year Treasury yield and the TIPS yield is read as the market's inflation expectation (the breakeven inflation rate).

    Why is gold sensitive to real rates?

    Someone holding gold earns no interest. Someone who puts the same money into a bond earns a return. That forgone return is the opportunity cost. When real rates rise, the opportunity cost of holding gold goes up; when real rates fall, especially below zero, that cost shrinks.

    What matters here is the real rate, not the nominal one. When inflation is high, a rise in nominal rates may not mean the same thing for gold as long as real rates stay low.

    Commonly observed tendencies

    • While real rates are rising, gold often comes under pressure; while real rates are falling, gold tends to find support.
    • Gold is priced in dollars on the international market. When the dollar strengthens, gold becomes more expensive for holders of other currencies, so a strong dollar often goes together with a weaker gold price.
    • Real rates and the dollar often move in the same direction; when both rise together, the pressure on gold can be more visible.
    • These relationships are tendencies. They often break down in daily and weekly moves and show more clearly over longer periods.

    When the relationship broke

    The inverse relationship has not always held. In the few years after 2022, real rates rose markedly while gold stayed strong instead of weakening. Strong central-bank gold buying is a frequently cited explanation for that period; geopolitical uncertainty and a wish to diversify reserves are also seen as factors.

    The picture can also change in sudden crises: the dollar and gold can rise at the same time on safe-haven demand, or gold can be sold along with everything else when cash is needed. So real rates and the dollar are only two of the factors that explain gold.

    Different pictures from the same data

    When real rates and the dollar move sharply on the same day, gold can react in several different ways.

    The expected way

    Real rates and the dollar fall and gold rises. The inverse relationship worked that day.

    The expected way, the other sign

    Real rates and the dollar rise and gold falls. The relationship worked again, this time against gold.

    A weak relationship

    Real rates rise but gold rises too or stays flat. Another factor (demand, uncertainty) may be stronger in that period.

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • The direction of the opportunity cost of holding gold
    • A likely source of macro pressure on, or support for, gold
    • Context to look at when reading a gold move

    What it does not prove

    • That a move in real rates or the dollar will push gold the other way
    • That the relationship will stay as strong in the next period
    • What level the gold price will reach

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    A sharp change in real rates, the dollar or inflation data can send the gold price quickly into a support or resistance zone. Whether the move is accepted at the zone or rejected is often read from the closes around the zone more than from the data itself.

    On data days, price can wick into a zone and out again. Reading the zone as a band rather than a single line, and looking at the 4H or daily close rather than the 1H, helps separate a brief spike from a lasting change.

    The link with crypto

    Real rates and the dollar can affect the crypto market too; both are important gauges of risk appetite. But gold and crypto do not always react to the same news in the same way. Moving together is a tendency, not a rule.

    Often confused with

    • Bond yields and the yield curveA nominal bond yield also contains inflation expectations; for gold the real yield (for example the TIPS yield) matters more.
    • The dollar index (DXY)The dollar index measures the dollar against a basket of currencies; its inverse link with gold is a tendency, not a fixed ratio.

    Key points

    • Real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation expectations; the most watched measure is the 10-year TIPS yield.
    • Gold pays no yield, so its opportunity cost changes with real rates.
    • Gold often tends to move against real rates and the dollar.
    • The relationship has weakened in some periods, for example during strong central-bank buying.
